strengths: The paper clearly motivates the need for cross-domain time-series saliency and positions CDIG well among prior work (VIL, MIX, FreqRISE, TIMING) with a useful transform-coverage table.

The complex-domain IG derivation provides completeness and path-independence guarantees, extending IG to complex transforms; the lemmas and proofs in the appendix are mostly rigorous and technically sound.

Empirical validation is diverse: controlled mechanistic analysis on a simple CNN, quantitative faithfulness benchmarks (CPD and insertion/deletion), and three real-world case studies in PPG heart-rate extraction, EEG seizure detection, and TimesFM forecasting.

The method is transform-agnostic and instantiated across six transform families (DFT, STFT, DWT, ICA, STL, Complex Cepstrum), with an open-source TensorFlow/PyTorch library and released code for reproducibility.
The limitations and impact statement are thoughtful, acknowledging baseline/path dependence, transform invertibility assumptions, and risks from inappropriate domain selection or over-interpretation.
Appendix connections showing equivalence to VIL for DFT and recovery of MIX for DWT help integrate the contribution with existing literature and clarify its relationship to prior methods.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is incremental for common real-valued transforms: CDIG is largely IG applied after an invertible change of variables, and for DFT it is shown equivalent to VIL; the main new technical piece is a Wirtinger-calculus extension to complex domains, which is a modest extension rather than a fundamentally new explanation method.

Baseline selection for the Complex Cepstrum is unclear and potentially problematic: T(0) is undefined because log(0) diverges, and the paper does not specify the baseline or inverse transform actually used, undermining reproducibility of the cepstrum results.

The invertibility/differentiability assumptions are not fully justified for some instantiations, especially ICA (data-estimated unmixing matrix, possible instability) and STL (non-trivial differentiation and inverse implementation are not detailed).

Algorithm pseudocode contains inconsistencies and possible errors (e.g., Algorithm 1 line 9 uses z before definition, Algorithm 2 line 6 applies T to z rather than x), and the treatment of autograd's conjugate Wirtinger derivative is not precise enough to guarantee faithful implementation.

Quantitative comparisons are somewhat limited: CPD uses only five repetitions without significance tests, insertion/deletion covers only two datasets and lacks main-text comparison to VIL/FreqRISE, and the forecasting evaluation is a single synthetic qualitative example.

The central claim that the explanation domain choice is consequential is illustrated but not systematically evaluated; the paper acknowledges the lack of metrics for domain appropriateness, but this leaves the main qualitative message less empirically grounded.

The method inherits IG's baseline and path sensitivity, yet only a zero baseline and linear path are explored; no sensitivity analysis quantifies how alternative baselines or non-linear paths affect attributions.

strengths: The paper targets a real and well-motivated gap: time-domain saliency maps for time series are often semantically uninterpretable, and framing the explanation domain as a task-dependent design choice (frequency, sources, trend/seasonality) is a sensible and useful framing.

The mathematical treatment of IG in transformed coordinates is internally consistent: Lemma 4.2, the Wirtinger-based derivation in Appendix C, and Definition 4.1 agree, and the completeness property f(x)-f(x̂)=Σ IG_i does hold as a consequence of the fundamental theorem of line integrals over the real-lift u:ℝ^{2n}→ℝ.

Broad empirical coverage: three real-world case studies spanning regression (PPG heart-rate), classification (EEG seizure detection), and forecasting (TimesFM zero-shot), across different architectures, plus quantitative faithfulness benchmarks against TIMEX++, TIMING, FreqRISE and VIL-style LRP/IG.

Reproducibility is reasonably supported: the transforms, datasets (PPG-Dalia, Siena, AudioMNIST), and models are specified, code is released, and the two complex-IG estimation algorithms are given in the appendix; limitations and an impact statement are provided and are honest.

The library contribution (TensorFlow/PyTorch, plug-and-play cross-domain explainability) is potentially useful to practitioners even if the underlying idea is a repackaging of transformed-coordinate attribution.
weaknesses: Novelty is substantially overstated relative to prior work, and the paper itself demonstrates this. Appendix E shows the DFT instantiation is algebraically equivalent to Virtual Inspection Layers, and Remark 4.4 states that the Haar-DWT case recovers MIX's view-space IG. The 'complex IG' is, by the paper's own Lemma 4.2, just standard real IG applied to the concatenated real/imaginary coordinates; consequently completeness and path-independence follow trivially from the fundamental theorem of line integrals and are not substantive theoretical results. The net contribution is a unifying wrapper plus instantiations, not a new attribution principle.

Theoretical framing contains an unjustified 'guarantee' claim: path-independence of the integral value is automatic for any gradient field, so presenting it as a theorem for complex IG is rhetorical rather than technical. Similarly, 'Proposition 3.1' (time domain is not always informative) is a restatement of prior empirical findings with no proof, yet is labeled and formatted as a proposition.

Evidence for the central claim is thin and partly circular. The flagship examples (Fourier for PPG, ICA for EEG, STL for forecasting) are precisely the domains practitioners already know are aligned, so 'time-domain methods cannot capture' these is largely expected; the only genuinely distinct complex-domain case (Cepstrum) is de-emphasized and supported mainly by an appendix benchmark.

The main quantitative comparison (Table 2) is not apples-to-apples: CDIG is allowed to select the best-performing transform per dataset, giving it an oracle advantage over fixed-domain baselines such as TIMING, while the most directly comparable method (VIL) is relegated to Appendix F, where CDIG is comparable to or worse than FreqRISE on faithfulness (e.g., Digit 0.19 vs 0.160; Gender 0.446 vs 0.416). On Epilepsy and Boiler (Fourier), TIMING still outperforms CDIG.

The faithfulness protocol (CPD / insertion-deletion) can be gamed by any attribution that points to features whose perturbation happens to produce large output changes, independent of faithfulness; the paper reports large advantages for Cepstrum in Table 2 without any control (e.g., random-feature or magnitude-matched baselines) to rule this out, which undermines the quantitative conclusions.

The mechanistic analysis in Section 4.2 is limited to single-channel, single-frequency sinusoids, and the synthetic TimesFM example (Appendix K) constructs the input from an additive exponential-trend-plus-sinusoid process that exactly matches STL's decomposition model, making the 'trend vs season' attribution demonstration somewhat self-fulfilling.

Presentation and reproducibility defects reduce confidence: the main text announces code 'available here' without a resolvable link; Algorithms 1–2 contain undefined or inconsistent variables (e.g., X vs z, unclear baseline handling, missing definition of Rz/Sz); and reference formatting is inconsistent throughout, with several entries garbled.

The paper's own limitation section concedes that the method is a sincere wrapper around IG (single baseline, straight-line path, invertible transforms only, requires correct domain choice), which further narrows the achieved contribution relative to the abstract and introduction claims about a 'generalization' of IG providing 'faithful attributions'.

strengths: Introduces Cross-domain Integrated Gradients, a principled generalization of IG to arbitrary invertible differentiable transforms, including complex-valued domains such as Fourier and complex cepstrum, with a derivation via Wirtinger calculus and real-lifting.

Provides theoretical support for completeness and path independence of the total attribution, and shows equivalence to VIL for DFT and to MIX's view-space IG for Haar-DWT, relating the framework to prior work.
Demonstrates broad practical utility across three real-world case studies (PPG heart rate, EEG seizure detection with ICA, TimesFM forecasting with STL) and multiple model architectures/tasks.

Reports quantitative faithfulness comparisons (CPD, insertion/deletion, AudioMNIST) showing competitive or better performance versus time-domain and frequency-domain baselines, with different transforms excelling on different datasets.
Releases an open-source TensorFlow/PyTorch library, includes detailed limitations, impact statement, and reproducibility-oriented appendices.
weaknesses: Although the complex-domain derivation is plausible, the paper overstates 'path independence' as an IG-style guarantee; total completeness is path-independent, but individual attributions depend on the chosen path, and the manuscript does not fully formalize additional IG axioms (e.g., sensitivity, implementation invariance) for the complex case.
Algorithm pseudocode in the appendix contains noticeable errors (e.g., z not initialized, X not used, T(z) typo in Algorithm 2), which hinders reproducibility and clarity.

Quantitative comparisons in the main text are limited to TIMEX++ and TIMING; stronger cross-domain baselines (e.g., VIL/FreqRISE) are mostly delegated to an appendix and only on one dataset, so the central empirical claim of broad cross-domain superiority is not fully established in the main text.
Several real-world evaluations rely on qualitative case studies or few samples and lack statistical significance tests/error bars (e.g., Tables 4 and 5), making it hard to assess robustness.

The method inherits common IG limitations (zero baseline, linear integration path, transform invertibility/domain choice) that can materially affect attributions; while acknowledged, these choices are not empirically explored.
